warmup.q: Payments 1, 3 and 5 of five are settled. This runs: payments.asSequence().filter { println("filter ${it.id}"); it.settled }.map { println("map ${it.id}"); it.amountCents }.take(2).toList(). What prints?
options: Nothing: a Sequence only runs when you print it
warmup.why: A Sequence pulls one payment through the whole chain before it reads the next one. Payment 1 passes the filter and goes straight on to map. Payment 2 fails the filter. Payment 3 passes and is mapped, and now take(2) has its two results, so nothing pulls payments 4 and 5. The first option is what the same chain prints on a List. toList() is what starts the work.

sections.h: A List chain builds a whole list at every step
sections.html:
Here is a scan from a fraud job. It asks a risk model to score each of the day's authorizations and returns the first one that looks bad.

Java
Auth firstSuspicious(List<Auth> feed) {
    List<Scored> scored = feed.stream().map(a -> new Scored(a, riskModel.score(a))).toList();   // 2 ms each
    List<Auth> flagged = scored.stream().filter(s -> s.score() >= 90).map(Scored::auth).toList();
    return flagged.isEmpty() ? null : flagged.get(0);
}
Kotlin
fun firstSuspicious(feed: List<Auth>): Auth? =
    feed.map { it to riskModel.score(it) }        // a 2 ms call per authorization
        .filter { (_, score) -> score >= 90 }
        .map { (auth, _) -> auth }
        .firstOrNull()

It reads well and gives the right answer. On a feed of a million authorizations where the first bad one is number 518, it also calls the model a million times. That is 33 minutes of model time to find something that was there after one second.

The cause is that map and filter on a Kotlin List are eager. Each one loops over its whole input, writes the results into a brand-new list, and only then does the next step start. So the first map scores all million and builds a list of a million pairs. filter builds a second list. firstOrNull finally looks at element 0. People call this horizontal: the work goes across every element for step 1, then across every element for step 2.

Java has no eager chain, so the Java version collects after every step to do the same thing. That is exactly what Kotlin's List operations do for you.

You saw in "Collections without loops: map, filter, fold and friends" that these functions are inline: the compiler pastes the loop and your lambda into the caller, so no lambda objects exist at run time. The cost is somewhere else. Every step allocates a new ArrayList, and a List<Long> holds boxed Long objects. In a JMH run made for this course, filter { }.map { }.sum() over a million payments allocated 26.5 MB per call.

For a short chain over a few hundred elements, none of this matters, and the eager version is the easiest to debug: you can stop after any step and look at a real list. It starts to matter when the input is big, the steps are expensive, or you only need the first few results.

try.title: Watch the order of the lambdas
steps: Open OrderDemo.kt (or OrderDemoJava.java). The same filter, map and take(2) run on a List and on a Sequence. Write down the print order you expect for each.
Run it with the command below.
In the List chain, move .take(2) up to right after txns. Predict how many filter lines print and what the result is, then run it.

Java has no eager chain, so the "List chain" collects after every step, * which is exactly what Kotlin's List operations do. try.expect: The List chain prints filter 1 to filter 5, then map 1, map 3, map 5: each step finishes before the next starts. The Sequence chain prints nothing until toList() (building it only made a TakeSequence), then filter 1, map 1, filter 2, filter 3, map 3. Payments 4 and 5 are never read. With take(2) first, the List chain filters only payments 1 and 2 and prints [1500]. That is a different question (which of the first two payments are settled), so moving a step changes the answer in both models. Laziness only changes how much work runs.

sections.h: A Sequence pulls one element through the whole chain
sections.html:
Put asSequence() in front of the same chain and the order of work changes. A Sequence is lazy: building the chain does nothing. The work starts at a terminal operation such as toList(), first(), sum() or count(), and then each element goes through every step before the next element is read. That is vertical order, and the figure shows it for five payments.

On the million authorizations, feed.asSequence().map { ... }.filter { ... }.map { ... }.firstOrNull() scores 518 and stops. This is short-circuiting: first, firstOrNull, any, find and take(n) can stop as soon as they have an answer, and in a lazy chain they stop every step above them too. For a single condition you don't even need a Sequence. feed.firstOrNull { risk(it) >= 90 } is one inlined loop, and it also stops at 518.

Underneath, each intermediate operation on a Sequence is an ordinary function, not inline, that wraps the previous sequence. map returns a TransformingSequence holding your lambda, filter a FilteringSequence, take a TakeSequence. When the terminal operation asks the last wrapper for an element, that wrapper asks the one before it, and so on up to the list. Here is the heart of TransformingSequence in the Kotlin 2.4.21 stdlib, next to the same idea written by hand in Java:

Java
Iterator<R> mapped = new Iterator<>() {
    public boolean hasNext() { return source.hasNext(); }
    public R next() { return transformer.apply(source.next()); }
};
Kotlin
override fun next(): R = transformer(iterator.next())
override fun hasNext(): Boolean = iterator.hasNext()

So a Sequence trades the intermediate lists for one small wrapper per step. The lambdas become real Function1 objects again (created through invokedynamic, as "Function types, lambdas and closures" showed), and a Long coming out of map is boxed on its way through invoke.

One kind of step breaks the vertical flow. sorted() and sortedBy { } must see every element before they can hand out the smallest, so the first request makes them copy the whole upstream into a list and sort it. In the Try it, a sortedBy before firstOrNull { } pulls all 1,000,000 authorizations, even though the model still runs only 518 times. If you only need the smallest element, minByOrNull { } reads the input once and sorts nothing.

try.title: Count the work on a million authorizations
steps: Read ScanCount.kt. Every line looks for the same authorization, number 518 of a million. For each line, predict how many times risk runs and how many authorizations the onEach counter pulls.
In the Sequence chain line, add .toList() just before .firstOrNull(). Predict the counts, then run it again.
Run the Java twin and compare findFirst on one Stream with collecting first.

code.title: ScanCount.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l05 data class Auth(val id: Long, val amountCents: Long) /** A million authorizations; the first suspicious one (over 20,000.00) is number 518. */ private val feed = List(1_000_000) { i -> Auth(i + 1L, if (i % 1_000 == 517) 2_500_000 else 1_000L + i % 90_000) } private var scored = 0 private var pulled = 0 /** Stands for a call to the fraud model. Counts every call. */ private fun risk(a: Auth): Int { scored++; return if (a.amountCents > 2_000_000) 95 else 10 } private fun report(label: String, found: Auth?) { println("%-22s scored %,9d pulled %,9d found id %s".format(label, scored, pulled, found?.id)) scored = 0; pulled = 0 } fun main() { report("List chain", feed.map { it to risk(it) }.filter { it.second >= 90 }.map { it.first }.firstOrNull()) report("Sequence chain", feed.asSequence().map { it to risk(it) }.filter { it.second >= 90 }.map { it.first }.firstOrNull()) report("Sequence + sortedBy", feed.asSequence().onEach { pulled++ }.sortedBy { it.id }.firstOrNull { risk(it) >= 90 }) report("firstOrNull { }", feed.firstOrNull { risk(it) >= 90 }) }

alt.title: ScanCountJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l05; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.List; import java.util.stream.IntStream; /** The same scan with Java collections and streams. The first suspicious authorization is number 518. */ public class ScanCountJava { record Auth(long id, long amountCents) {} record Scored(Auth auth, int score) {} static final List<Auth> FEED = IntStream.range(0, 1_000_000) .mapToObj(i -> new Auth(i + 1L, i % 1_000 == 517 ? 2_500_000 : 1_000L + i % 90_000)) .toList(); static int scored = 0; static int pulled = 0; /** Stands for a call to the fraud model. Counts every call. */ static int risk(Auth a) { scored++; return a.amountCents() > 2_000_000 ? 95 : 10; } static void report(String label, Auth found) { System.out.printf("%-22s scored %,9d pulled %,9d found id %s%n", label, scored, pulled, found == null ? null : found.id()); scored = 0; pulled = 0; } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Scored> all = FEED.stream().map(a -> new Scored(a, risk(a))).toList(); // collect first, like a List chain report("Collect, then search", all.stream().filter(s -> s.score() >= 90).map(Scored::auth).findFirst().orElse(null)); report("One Stream", FEED.stream().map(a -> new Scored(a, risk(a))).filter(s -> s.score() >= 90) .map(Scored::auth).findFirst().orElse(null)); report("Stream + sorted", FEED.stream().peek(a -> pulled++).sorted(Comparator.comparingLong(Auth::id)) .filter(a -> risk(a) >= 90).findFirst().orElse(null)); } }

try.expect: The List chain scores all 1,000,000. The Sequence chain and firstOrNull { } score 518 and stop. The sortedBy line also scores only 518, but its counter shows it pulled all 1,000,000 into a list to sort them first. With .toList() added, the Sequence scores 1,000,000 again: toList() is a terminal operation that wants every element. Java prints the same numbers, because a Stream is lazy in the same way and a collected list is not.

sections.h: Make your own: generateSequence and sequence { yield }
sections.html:
A Sequence doesn't need a collection behind it. Two builders produce elements only when someone asks.

generateSequence(seed) { next } computes each element from the one before and ends when the lambda returns null. Here is a retry schedule that doubles from 100 ms up to 1.6 s:

Java
List<Long> backoff = Stream.iterate(100L, d -> d <= 1_600, d -> d * 2).toList();   // [100, 200, 400, 800, 1600]
Kotlin
val backoff = generateSequence(100L) { (it * 2).takeIf { next -> next <= 1_600 } }
backoff.toList()   // [100, 200, 400, 800, 1600]

Without the takeIf, the sequence is infinite. That is fine as long as something downstream stops it, such as take(5) or first { }.

sequence { } is for when making the next element takes real code, like a paging API. Inside the block, yield(x) hands out one element and yieldAll(list) hands out many:

Java
Stream<Settlement> settlements = Stream.iterate(1, page -> page <= 3, page -> page + 1)
        .flatMap(page -> fetchPage(page).stream());
settlements.filter(s -> s.amountCents() > 6_500).findFirst();   // also skips page 3 on JDK 21
Kotlin
val settlements = sequence {
    for (page in 1..3) yieldAll(fetchPage(page))   // fetchPage is an HTTP call
}
settlements.first { it.amountCents > 6_500 }       // fetches page 1 and page 2, never page 3

How does a for loop stop halfway? The block is a suspend lambda (its type is suspend SequenceScope<T>.() -> Unit). The compiler turns it into a state machine, the same way it compiles the suspend functions in the coroutines track. Each yield saves where the block is and returns control to the consumer. When the consumer asks for the next element, the block resumes right after that yield. No thread is involved: it all runs on the caller's thread, one step at a time. When the consumer stops asking, the block never resumes, so page 3 is never requested.

The scope is restricted. Only yield and yieldAll may suspend in there. Call delay inside sequence { } and Kotlin 2.4.21 refuses: Restricted suspending functions can invoke member or extension suspending functions only on their restricted coroutine scope. For paging that has to wait without blocking, use a Flow (the coroutines track).

The lab's paging source has one more rule: it doesn't know how many pages exist, and an empty page means the end. In Kotlin that is a while (true) loop with a break. In Java it is Stream.iterate(0, p -> p + 1).map(api::page).takeWhile(p -> !p.isEmpty()).flatMap(List::stream).

try.title: Fetch only the pages you read
steps: Read Paging.kt. Each page holds three settlements. Predict which pages are fetched before the first settlement over 65.00 prints.
Change first to firstOrNull and the threshold to 1_000_000. Predict which pages are fetched and what prints, then run it.

code.title: Paging.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l05 data class Settlement(val ref: String, val amountCents: Long) /** Stands for one HTTP call to the acquirer: three pages of settlement records. */ private fun fetchPage(page: Int): List<Settlement> { println(" fetching page $page") return List(3) { i -> Settlement("S$page-$i", (page * 3 + i) * 1_000L) } } fun main() { // 1. a paging source: the block runs only as far as the consumer pulls val settlements = sequence { for (page in 1..3) yieldAll(fetchPage(page)) } println("first settlement over 65.00:") println(" ${settlements.first { it.amountCents > 6_500 }}") // 2. a retry schedule: 100 ms doubling, and the sequence ends when the lambda returns null val backoff = generateSequence(100L) { (it * 2).takeIf { next -> next <= 1_600 } } println("backoff: ${backoff.toList()}") }

alt.title: PagingJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l05; import java.util.List; import java.util.stream.IntStream; import java.util.stream.Stream; /** The same paging source and retry schedule with Java streams (JDK 9+ for the three-argument iterate). */ public class PagingJava { record Settlement(String ref, long amountCents) {} /** Stands for one HTTP call to the acquirer: three pages of settlement records. */ static List<Settlement> fetchPage(int page) { System.out.println(" fetching page " + page); return IntStream.range(0, 3).mapToObj(i -> new Settlement("S" + page + "-" + i, (page * 3 + i) * 1_000L)).toList(); } public static void main(String[] args) { // 1. a paging source: a stream of page numbers, flattened into records Stream<Settlement> settlements = Stream.iterate(1, page -> page <= 3, page -> page + 1) .flatMap(page -> fetchPage(page).stream()); System.out.println("first settlement over 65.00:"); System.out.println(" " + settlements.filter(s -> s.amountCents() > 6_500).findFirst().orElseThrow()); // 2. a retry schedule: seed, condition to continue, next value List<Long> backoff = Stream.iterate(100L, delay -> delay <= 1_600, delay -> delay * 2).toList(); System.out.println("backoff: " + backoff); } }

try.expect: fetching page 1, fetching page 2, then Settlement(ref=S2-1, amountCents=7000). Page 3 is never fetched, because first stopped asking. With no match, all three pages are fetched and it prints null: laziness can only save work when something stops early. The backoff line is [100, 200, 400, 800, 1600] in both languages.

sections.h: Sequence or Stream, and when you need neither
sections.html:
A Java Stream is lazy and vertical, just like a Sequence. The Java twins in this lesson print the same order and the same counts. The differences are practical.

A Sequence is a recipe. Each terminal operation runs the whole chain again, side effects included: call sum() and then count() on the same sequence and every map lambda runs twice. A few sequences refuse a second run. iterator().asSequence() and generateSequence { } without a seed throw IllegalStateException: This sequence can be consumed only once. A Stream is always single-use. The second terminal operation throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed.

Streams can do things sequences can't. parallelStream() splits the work over the common ForkJoinPool, and sequences have no parallel mode at all. LongStream and mapToLong keep primitives unboxed, and Kotlin has no LongSequence. On JDK 24 and later, Gatherers add windowing and scans to streams.

Here are the numbers from the JMH run behind this course. The machine was a 4-vCPU VM shared with other work, so treat the times as rough. The bytes allocated per call barely move between runs, so you can trust those. It summed settled amounts over 1,000,000 payments:

Variant Time per call Allocated per call
for loop 5.2 ms about 0
filter { }.map { }.sum() on a List 148 ms 26,507,194 B
sumOf { if (settled) amount else 0L } 2.6 ms about 0
asSequence().filter { }.map { }.sum() 9.0 ms 189 B
stream().filter().mapToLong().sum() 8.9 ms 428 B
stream().filter().map().reduce(0L, ...) 14 ms 28,782,178 B

The fastest line is neither a List chain nor a Sequence: it is one fused sumOf, which is the hand-written loop. The Sequence allocated almost nothing only because the JIT removed the boxes in this tiny benchmark. Don't count on that in a large service where one call site sees many different lambdas. When the terminal operation could stop early (first match at index 101), the gap was huge: 141 ns for the Sequence, 4.4 ms for the List chain.

So here is the rule I use. Use List operations by default. Switch to asSequence() when the terminal operation can stop early, or when a long chain runs over a large input. Use sequence { } or generateSequence for data that is produced on demand, such as pages and retries. Use a Stream when you need parallel(), a primitive stream or a Gatherer, or when a Java API hands you one. And when one pass does the job, write one pass: sumOf, count { }, firstOrNull { }.

try.title: Run a sequence twice, and a stream twice
steps: Read Reuse.kt. Predict how many map lines print, and what the second read of once does.
In Reuse.kt, delete .asSequence() from amounts. Predict how many map lines print now.

code.title: Reuse.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l05 data class Refund(val id: Int, val amountCents: Long) private val refunds = listOf(Refund(1, 500), Refund(2, 1_200), Refund(3, 300)) fun main() { // 1. a sequence is a recipe: every terminal operation runs the whole chain again val amounts = refunds.asSequence().map { println(" map ${it.id}"); it.amountCents } println("sum = ${amounts.sum()}") println("count = ${amounts.count()}") // 2. some sequences can be read only once val once = refunds.iterator().asSequence() println("first read: ${once.map { it.id }.toList()}") try { once.toList() } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("second read: ${e::class.simpleName}: ${e.message}") } }

alt.title: ReuseJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l05; import java.util.List; import java.util.stream.Stream; /** A Java Stream is always single-use: the second terminal operation throws. */ public class ReuseJava { record Refund(int id, long amountCents) {} public static void main(String[] args) { List<Refund> refunds = List.of(new Refund(1, 500), new Refund(2, 1_200), new Refund(3, 300)); Stream<Long> amounts = refunds.stream().map(r -> { System.out.println(" map " + r.id()); return r.amountCents(); }); System.out.println("sum = " + amounts.mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum()); try { System.out.println("count = " + amounts.count()); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("count again: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage()); } // to run it again, build a new stream from the source System.out.println("count = " + refunds.stream().count()); } }

try.expect: Six map lines: three for sum() and three more for count(), because each terminal operation reruns the chain. The iterator-backed sequence fails on its second read with IllegalStateException: This sequence can be consumed only once. Java's stream fails on the second terminal operation with IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. Without asSequence(), amounts is a List built once, so map prints three lines in total.

analogy: A List chain is a mailroom clerk who stamps every letter in the sack, then sorts every stamped letter, then delivers. A Sequence clerk takes one letter, stamps it, sorts it, delivers it, and only then reaches for the next one, so when you say "I only need the first two delivered" the rest of the sack stays untouched. The lazy clerk also does nothing at all until someone asks for a delivery. The analogy breaks in one place: a clerk who is told to sort the sack by postcode can't deliver anything until every letter is out of the sack. That is sorted() in a Sequence, and no amount of laziness avoids it.
world: Paging is where this pays off in a payments service. A Quarkus scheduled job that reconciles with an acquirer often reads a settlement API page by page: sequence { } with yieldAll(page) lets the rest of the job be plain filter, map and first while only the pages it reads are fetched. A Kafka consumer's poll loop is the opposite case: a batch of 500 records is already in memory, so a List chain is simpler and just as fast. Inside a Temporal activity, keep the laziness inside the activity. A Sequence is a recipe, not data: pass the materialized result (toList()) out of the activity, never the sequence.
mistake:
The most common real mistake is returning a lazy sequence that reads from a resource you have already closed:

Java
Stream<Refund> refunds(DataSource ds) throws SQLException {
    try (Connection c = ds.getConnection()) {
        ResultSet rs = c.prepareStatement("select id, amount from refund").executeQuery();
        return Stream.generate(() -> next(rs)).takeWhile(Objects::nonNull);
    }   // closed here, before the caller's terminal operation runs
}
Kotlin
fun refunds(ds: DataSource): Sequence<Refund> = ds.connection.use { c ->
    val rs = c.prepareStatement("select id, amount from refund").executeQuery()
    generateSequence { if (rs.next()) Refund(rs.getLong(1), rs.getLong(2)) else null }
}   // use { } closes the connection here, before anyone reads the sequence

It compiles and looks tidy. The first read fails later, far from this code, because the connection is gone. People make it because the code looks like it fetches the rows inside use, but a lazy chain only describes the work. Either finish the work inside the block (.toList() before the closing brace, if the result fits in memory), or turn it around and take the consumer as a parameter: fun forEachRefund(ds: DataSource, action: (Refund) -> Unit), so the reading happens while the connection is open.

compare.title: The first suspicious foreign payments: Sequence vs Stream

java.title: FraudScan.java
java.html: List<Long> firstSuspiciousForeign(List<Payment> feed, ToIntFunction<Payment> riskScore, int n) { return feed.stream() .filter(p -> !p.country().equals("NL")) // cheap check first .filter(p -> riskScore.applyAsInt(p) >= 90) .map(Payment::id) // boxed Long, as in Kotlin .limit(n) // short-circuits like take(n) .toList(); // unmodifiable on JDK 16+ }

kotlin.title: FraudScan.kt
kotlin.html: fun firstSuspiciousForeign(feed: List<Payment>, riskScore: (Payment) -> Int, n: Int): List<Long> = feed.asSequence() .filter { it.country != "NL" } // cheap check first .filter { riskScore(it) >= 90 } .map { it.id } // boxed Long at the Function1 boundary .take(n) // short-circuits like limit(n) .toList()

compare.note: Both pipelines are lazy and run in the same vertical order, so both call the model exactly as often. The real differences are around the edges. The Stream can only be consumed once; the Sequence can be iterated again and will rerun the whole chain. The Stream could go parallel(); the Sequence can't. Kotlin's terminal operations mirror the List API (firstOrNull returns null, groupBy, sumOf), while the Stream returns Optional from findFirst and needs Collectors for grouping. And on the Kotlin side you can drop asSequence() and get an eager List chain with the same code, which is often the better choice for small inputs.

worked.title: Decide whether a reconciliation report should be lazy

steps.say: A nightly reconciliation compares 2 million ledger lines with the acquirer's file and alerts on the first 20 mismatches. Here is the first version. Before reading on, find the step that makes laziness pay off.
steps.code: fun firstMismatches(ledger: List<LedgerLine>, acquirer: Map<String, Long>): List<Mismatch> = ledger.map { line -> Mismatch(line.ref, line.amountCents, acquirer[line.ref]) } .filter { it.acquirerCents != it.ledgerCents } .take(20)

alt.html: List<Mismatch> firstMismatches(List<LedgerLine> ledger, Map<String, Long> acquirer) { List<Mismatch> all = ledger.stream() .map(line -> new Mismatch(line.ref(), line.amountCents(), acquirer.get(line.ref()))) .toList(); // 2 million objects return all.stream().filter(m -> !Objects.equals(m.acquirerCents(), m.ledgerCents())).limit(20).toList(); }

steps.say: take(20) can stop early, so this chain should be lazy. 1. Ask the question: does the terminal step stop before the end? Here, yes. 2. Put asSequence() at the front. Now the chain builds 20 mismatches plus the matching lines it read on the way, and no 2-million-element lists.
steps.code: fun firstMismatches(ledger: List<LedgerLine>, acquirer: Map<String, Long>): List<Mismatch> = ledger.asSequence() // 2. lazy from here on .map { line -> Mismatch(line.ref, line.amountCents, acquirer[line.ref]) } .filter { it.acquirerCents != it.ledgerCents } .take(20) // 1. stops early .toList()

alt.html: List<Mismatch> firstMismatches(List<LedgerLine> ledger, Map<String, Long> acquirer) { return ledger.stream() // 2. one lazy pipeline .map(line -> new Mismatch(line.ref(), line.amountCents(), acquirer.get(line.ref()))) .filter(m -> !Objects.equals(m.acquirerCents(), m.ledgerCents())) .limit(20) // 1. stops early .toList(); }

steps.say: 1. Move cheap checks before expensive ones. Building a Mismatch for every line is wasted work; compare first and build the object only for real mismatches.
steps.code: ledger.asSequence() .filter { acquirer[it.ref] != it.amountCents } // 3. cheap test, no allocation .map { Mismatch(it.ref, it.amountCents, acquirer[it.ref]) } .take(20) .toList()

alt.html: ledger.stream() .filter(l -> !Objects.equals(acquirer.get(l.ref()), l.amountCents())) // 3. cheap test .map(l -> new Mismatch(l.ref(), l.amountCents(), acquirer.get(l.ref()))) .limit(20) .toList();

steps.say: 1. Look for a barrier. Product now asks for the 20 largest mismatches. That needs sortedByDescending { } before take(20), and the sort must read all 2 million lines first, so the Sequence saves nothing over a List here. Keep whichever is easier to read, and know that the cost is the full pass plus the sort.
steps.code: ledger.asSequence() .filter { acquirer[it.ref] != it.amountCents } .sortedByDescending { abs(it.amountCents - (acquirer[it.ref] ?: 0L)) } // 4. reads everything .take(20) .map { Mismatch(it.ref, it.amountCents, acquirer[it.ref]) } .toList()

alt.html: ledger.stream() .filter(l -> !Objects.equals(acquirer.get(l.ref()), l.amountCents())) .sorted(Comparator.comparingLong((LedgerLine l) -> Math.abs(l.amountCents() - acquirer.getOrDefault(l.ref(), 0L))).reversed()) .limit(20) // 4. sorted() already read everything .map(l -> new Mismatch(l.ref(), l.amountCents(), acquirer.get(l.ref()))) .toList();

lab.title: Score only what you must, and page lazily
steps: Run the tests. Seven of nine fail. firstSuspicious already returns the right payment, but the test shows it calls the model 200,000 times.
Fix firstSuspicious so it scores only up to the first match. Keep the signature.
Write firstSuspiciousForeign: domestic ("NL") cards must never reach the model, and nothing may be scored after the nth match.
Write allSettlements with sequence { }: ask for page 0, then 1, then 2, and stop at the first empty page.
Run the tests until all nine pass. Then read the last test and say what it shows about iterating a sequence twice.
hints: For firstSuspicious, feed.asSequence() in front of the existing chain is enough. So is feed.firstOrNull { riskScore(it) >= 90 }, one inlined loop.
In firstSuspiciousForeign, the order of the two filter calls decides which payments reach the model. take(n) goes after both, before toList().
Inside sequence { } a while (true) loop is fine: break on an empty page, otherwise yieldAll(page). The loop pauses at every yieldAll until the consumer wants more.

drill.title: A paging source from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write fun <T> paged(fetch: (Int) -> List<T>): Sequence<T> that asks for page 1, then 2, then 3, and so on, and stops at the first empty page without asking for the next one. Then write the Java version that returns a Stream<T>. Check: does yours fetch anything before a terminal operation runs?

answer.html: fun <T> paged(fetch: (Int) -> List<T>): Sequence<T> = sequence { var page = 1 while (true) { val items = fetch(page++) // runs only when the consumer asks for more if (items.isEmpty()) break // an empty page ends it yieldAll(items) // pauses here between elements } }

alt.html: static <T> Stream<T> paged(IntFunction<List<T>> fetch) { return Stream.iterate(1, page -> page + 1) // 1, 2, 3, ... lazily .map(fetch::apply) // one fetch per page, on demand .takeWhile(items -> !items.isEmpty()) // stops at the first empty page .flatMap(List::stream); }

recap: List operations are eager: each step loops over everything and builds a new list. They are inlined, so the cost is the lists and the boxing, not lambda objects.
A Sequence is lazy: nothing runs until a terminal operation, then each element passes through every step before the next is read.
Laziness pays when the terminal step stops early (first, any, take). sorted reads the whole upstream first.
generateSequence and sequence { yield } produce elements on demand; yield suspends the block on the caller's thread until the next request.
A Sequence reruns its chain on every terminal operation (a few are once-only); a Java Stream is always single-use but can go parallel and stay unboxed.
Default to List operations; use a Sequence for early exits, long chains on big inputs and paging; one fused sumOf or firstOrNull { } beats both.

explain.prompt: A teammate added .asSequence() in front of every collection chain in the settlement service "because sequences are faster". Explain in your own words what a Sequence changes, and when it is worth it.
explain.answer: A Sequence changes the order of work. A List chain runs each step over the whole collection and builds a new list before the next step starts. A Sequence runs nothing until a terminal operation asks for elements, then moves each element through every step before reading the next. That saves the intermediate lists, and when the last step can stop early, like first or take, it skips the rest of the input entirely. It isn't free: each step becomes a wrapper object with a lambda, values get boxed through invoke, and a chain run twice does all its work twice. For a full pass over a few hundred elements, the eager chain is just as fast and easier to debug, and a single sumOf or count { } beats both. I'd keep asSequence() where a chain stops early or runs several steps over large inputs, and remove it elsewhere.

deeper.html:
Three details that matter once you write sequences in hot code.

Boxing. A Sequence of Long is a sequence of java.lang.Long objects, because each step calls a Function1 whose invoke takes and returns Object. In bytecode, the lambda of map { it.amountCents } is a Function1 whose invokedynamic signature returns Ljava/lang/Long;. Java's mapToLong takes a ToLongFunction that returns a primitive long. In the JMH run above, the Sequence still allocated only 189 bytes per call, because C2's escape analysis saw that the boxes never escaped and removed them. That worked because the benchmark had one call site and one lambda type. In a real service the same FilteringSequence code runs with dozens of different lambdas, its call site becomes megamorphic, the JIT stops inlining, and the boxes come back.

IntelliJ's hint. The Kotlin plugin has an inspection that suggests converting a call chain on a collection into a sequence. It is on by default as a weak warning and fires for chains of five or more calls. Treat it as a prompt to ask the question from this lesson (does the end of the chain stop early, and is the input big?), not as a rule.

Gatherers. Since JDK 24, streams have Stream.gather, with built-ins in java.util.stream.Gatherers: windowFixed, windowSliding, fold, scan and mapConcurrent. Kotlin has had the equivalents on both List and Sequence for years: chunked, windowed, fold and runningFold (also called scan). So on JDK 21, a 7-day moving average of settlement volume is days.windowed(7) { it.average() } in Kotlin and a hand-written loop in Java; on JDK 24 and later Java can write stream.gather(Gatherers.windowSliding(7)). The labs compile with release 21, so they use none of this.
